Tile the M-dimension (i) with factor 128. This creates 512/128=4 outer tiles along M. Combined with J tiling this gives thread-blocks of 128×128 output elements — a standard large-GEMM tile that maximises arithmetic intensity and reuse of A rows from shared memory while fitting within the 49 KB SMEM budget on Ampere.

Tile the N-dimension (j) with factor 128. Creates 4 outer tiles along N, giving a 4×4=16 output-block grid across 30 SMs for good occupancy. The 128×128 output tile drives high register reuse for B columns. Together i=128, j=128 provides the canonical GEMM tile that amortises DRAM traffic.

Tile the K reduction axis with factor 32. This sets the shared-memory staging depth: each iteration loads a 128×32 slice of A and a 32×128 slice of B into SMEM (128×32×2 bytes × 2 = 32 KB for FP32 — well within 49 KB), enabling the outer K loop to stream through the full K=512 in 16 steps while keeping data in fast SMEM.

Map the outer i-tile loop (4 tiles of 128) to threadblock.x. This distributes the M-dimension work across SM grid columns, enabling 4 independent thread-blocks along M to run concurrently on separate SMs.

Map the outer j-tile loop (4 tiles of 128) to threadblock.y. Combined with i→threadblock.x, this creates a 4×4=16 thread-block grid which covers all 30 SMs with two waves (first 16 blocks + 14 from a second wave), giving high SM utilization for the 512×512 problem.

Vectorize the inner j loop with width=4. On Ampere this emits 128-bit (float4) memory loads/stores, maximising memory-bus utilization and enabling the hardware's memory coalescing. Width 4 is the sweet-spot that fits register capacity within a 128-wide j tile.

Unroll the inner k loop by factor 4. With k tile=32, this unrolls 4 iterations of the inner-most accumulation loop, reducing loop-control overhead and enabling the instruction scheduler to hide latency through instruction-level parallelism (ILP) across the 4 unrolled FMAs.

Map the inner i-loop (128 elements) to warp-level parallelism. This subdivides the i-tile among warps within each thread-block, exposing 128/32=4 warps along M. Combined with j on threadblock.y, this enables warp-level data partitioning that keeps each warp's register file busy and allows the SM scheduler to hide memory-access latency via warp interleaving.

Unroll the inner i-loop by factor 4 to expose ILP along the M-dimension within each warp's register tile. Each unrolled iteration computes a separate row accumulator, and the compiler/scheduler can overlap independent FMA chains — reducing the effective critical-path latency of the reduction loop.

Unroll the inner j-loop by factor 4 to complement the j-vectorization (width=4 × unroll=4 = 16 j-elements per thread iteration). This exposes 4 independent FMA chains along the N-dimension per warp, saturating the Ampere SM's dual FP32 FMA pipelines and hiding pipeline latency.

Tiling i by 128 creates 4 output row-blocks for a 512-row matrix. A 128-row tile fits well in shared memory and gives each threadblock a large compute chunk, improving data reuse of the A-tile across the k-reduction and reducing DRAM traffic.

Tiling j by 128 creates 4 output column-blocks. A 128×128 output tile matches the classic cuBLAS-style block size for square matmuls; the 128×128 C-block stays in registers while A[128×k] and B[k×128] tiles rotate through shared memory, achieving high arithmetic intensity (~10.9 FLOPs/byte at fp32).

Map the tiled i-outer loop to threadblock.x so each SM receives an independent row-block of the output. With 4 i-blocks × 4 j-blocks = 16 threadblocks, all 30 SMs will be kept busy (some get 0–1 blocks; doubling to 128-tile gives better occupancy than larger tiles).

Map the tiled j-outer loop to threadblock.y to form a 2D grid of (i_blocks × j_blocks) = 4×4 = 16 threadblocks. 2D grid layout preserves locality: adjacent blocks share rows of A (threadblock.x) or columns of B (threadblock.y), reducing L2 cache pressure.

Tile i by 64 creates 8 row-blocks. Combined with 8 j-blocks (64-tile), we get 64 threadblocks — more than double the 30 SMs, giving ≥2 waves and good occupancy. A 64×64 output tile also has a more favorable register pressure vs. 128×128.

Tile j by 64 to match i, completing a 64×64 output block. This symmetric tiling keeps A and B shared memory tiles square (64×k_tile), which balances bandwidth for both operands and is a well-known sweet spot for Ampere matmul kernels.
Map i-outer (8 blocks) to threadblock.x. Combining with j-outer on threadblock.y yields an 8×8 = 64 block grid, ensuring all 30 SMs are kept busy with ≥2 blocks each — maximizing SM utilization.
Map j-outer (8 blocks) to threadblock.y to complete the 2D 8×8 SM grid. This co-locates blocks that share the same B column tiles under threadblock.y, enhancing L2 reuse for B's columns.

Vectorize the j (column) inner loop with width 4 (128-bit loads for fp32). This enables LDG.128 global loads for B's row slices and STS.128 shared-memory stores, which are the widest efficient memory transactions on Ampere and hide memory latency better than scalar loads.

Tile the outer row dimension 'i' by 32. This maps 32 rows per block — with M=2048 rows that gives 64 blocks across 30 SMs (≈2.1 waves), maximizing SM utilization while keeping per-block shared memory manageable for the row-wise reduction.

Tile the reduction dimension 'j' by 128. N=2048 elements split into 16 tiles of 128 — each tile fits a warp (128/4 = 32 float4 vectorized loads). This enables 128-bit memory accesses and creates the inner loop structure needed for vectorize and unroll decisions next.

Map the outer 'i' tile to threadblock.x — each CUDA block processes a tile of 32 rows. With 2048/32=64 blocks launched across 30 SMs, this gives full SM utilization and maps naturally to the row-independent parallelism of RMSNorm.

Map the inner 'j' tiles to warps within the block. Each warp handles a 128-element strip of the N=2048 reduction, enabling warp-level shuffle-based reduction (shfl.xor) rather than slower shared-memory atomics. 2048/128=16 warps per block × 32 threads = 512 threads/block — well within the 1024 limit.

Vectorize the j-loop with width=4 (float4 = 128-bit loads). This maximizes memory bandwidth utilization on Ampere (which has 128-bit wide memory buses) and reduces instruction count by 4×. With j-tile=128 and vec=4, each thread issues 128/4=32 vectorized load instructions — a good balance for the instruction cache.

Unroll the j inner loop by 8. With j-tile=128 and vec=4, the innermost loop has 128/4=32 iterations; unrolling by 8 leaves 4 meta-iterations and exposes 8 independent accumulators to the compiler — critical for hiding the 4-cycle FP32 latency on Ampere and saturating the CUDA cores with independent FP ops.

Tile 'i' by 1 — one row per block. With M=2048 rows this launches 2048 blocks, saturating all 30 SMs with ~68 concurrent blocks per SM. This is the canonical RMSNorm/LayerNorm pattern: one block = one row, so all threads within the block cooperate on the single row's reduction, enabling efficient warp shuffles and maximizing parallelism.

Start with 256 threads/block. For N=4096, this means 16 elements per thread, giving good arithmetic intensity per thread while keeping occupancy high (multiple blocks can co-reside on each SM). This is a balanced starting point between the extremes.

Try 512 threads/block. For N=4096, this means 8 elements per thread with a single warp reduction step less. 512 threads fills half the max block capacity — may hit better occupancy/register-pressure tradeoff than 256, especially on a 30-SM Ampere with 49 KB shared memory.

Try the maximum 1024 threads/block. For N=4096, each thread handles exactly 4 elements. 1024 threads = 32 warps per block saturates the SM's warp scheduler; the per-row reduction is fully contained within one block, minimizing inter-block sync and maximizing L1/shared-memory reuse of W and B. This is the classic high-throughput layernorm configuration.

Try the minimum 128 threads/block. For N=4096 this means 32 elements per thread — highest arithmetic intensity per thread and most blocks per SM (more concurrent blocks), potentially better latency hiding. Worth measuring as the opposite extreme from 1024.

Vectorize the inner reduction loop (j) with width=4. For float32, this maps to 128-bit (float4) loads — the widest coalesced access that fits in a single instruction on Ampere. N=4096 is divisible by 4, making this safe. This should improve memory bandwidth utilization during the row-wise reads of X, W, and B.

Try maximum vectorization width=8 on the j (reduction) loop. This is 256-bit load per thread, which may amortize address calculation overhead further. N=4096 is divisible by 8, so it is safe. Combined with 512 threads this gives 4096/(512*8)=1 chunk per thread — extremely coalesced.

Place the W (scale) tensor in shared memory. W[4096] is read once per output element per row — with 1024 rows, it's accessed M times total. Placing it in shared memory (49KB available) allows the 512 threads to load W cooperatively and reuse across iterations, reducing global memory pressure.

Unroll the inner j loop by factor 8 to expose more ILP to the scheduler. With 512 threads and N=4096, each thread handles 8 elements; fully unrolling this means 8 independent FMA chains, hiding memory latency and improving instruction-level parallelism across the reduction pass.

Stack vectorize(j, width=4) on top of unroll(j, 8) + block_threads(512). The combination of unrolling (ILP) and vectorization (memory throughput) together may further reduce latency compared to either alone.

Explicitly map the outer row dimension i to threadblock.x. LayerNorm is trivially parallel across rows; making this mapping explicit may help the compiler generate better grid-launch code and expose more SM-level parallelism across the 1024 rows with 30 SMs available.

Try unrolling the outer i (row) loop by 4. This processes 4 rows per block iteration, enabling the compiler to interleave memory accesses for different rows and better pipeline the loads, potentially improving throughput across the M=1024 dimension.
Re-apply 512 threads as the closest-to-default performer (vs_default ~1.002), as the base for further combinator search.

LayerNorm is row-wise over N=4096. With 512 threads/block, each thread handles 4096/512=8 elements — enough arithmetic intensity to hide memory latency while keeping 2 blocks/SM (512*2=1024 ≤ max_threads_per_block=1024). This is the canonical sweet-spot for a reduce of this width on Ampere.

Try 256 threads/block: each thread handles 4096/256=16 elements (more work per thread, better register reuse). With 30 SMs and M=32 rows, each SM gets ~1 block; 256 threads leaves headroom for higher occupancy via multiple blocks per SM. Likely less warp-divergence overhead in the reduction tree too.

Try 1024 threads/block: maximum occupancy per block, each thread covers 4096/1024=4 elements. With M=32 rows and 30 SMs, we get ~1 block/SM; the full warp-parallel reduction over 32 warps can exploit all Ampere warp-shuffle hardware efficiently and maximise memory bandwidth utilisation across the wide N=4096 row.

Complete the sweep: try 128 threads/block, the smallest option. Each thread handles 4096/128=32 elements — most work per thread but fewest parallel threads. Useful to confirm whether under-parallelism is worse than 1024.

Start with the largest balanced tile (WM=4, WN=4) with asymmetric warp tiles (WTM=2, WTN=4). This maximizes the output tile area per warp (4x4 WMMA fragments × 2×4 warp tiles = large data reuse), which is critical for hiding memory latency on a 1024×1024 square matmul. The top candidate in the list suggests the compiler ranks this highly.

Try WTM=4, WTN=2 variant (transposed warp tile ratio vs previous). For a square matmul, column-major warp tiling can change how shared memory is accessed; may reduce bank conflicts on the M-dimension by using wider warp tiles along M.

Try mid-range block tiles WM=2,WN=2 with WTM=2,WTN=4. Smaller block tiles reduce shared memory pressure and allow more blocks in flight on 30 SMs, potentially improving occupancy for a 1024x1024 matmul. This is in the middle of the size range and worth probing.

WM=4,WN=4 maximum block tiles with WTM=1,WTN=4 — skinny warp tiles. This configuration keeps the large block-level tile (best for data reuse across the K dimension) but uses narrow per-warp tiles. May reduce register pressure vs WTM=2/4 variants while preserving L1/shared memory utilization.

Symmetric WM=4,WN=4,WTM=2,WTN=2 — perfectly balanced block and warp tiles for a square 1024x1024 matmul. Equal M/N tiling avoids asymmetric memory access patterns and may produce the best cache line alignment for both A and B.

Software pipelining depth=2 enables double-buffering in shared memory: while one tile is being computed by the WMMA units, the next tile is being prefetched. This effectively hides global→shared memory latency, which is critical on Ampere where async copy instructions (cp.async) are available.
Same symmetric large tile as best config; now testing pipeline depth=3 to see if triple-buffering outperforms double-buffering on Ampere.

Triple-buffering (depth=3): allows even more overlap between compute and memory fetches. On Ampere, if register file is large enough, deeper pipelining can further reduce stall cycles. Testing against depth=2 baseline.
Same symmetric large tile, now testing pipeline depth=4 (quad-buffering) to explore the full pipeline range.
Test quad-buffering (depth=4): deeper pipeline may help on Ampere with async memory copy instructions, but also uses more shared memory — checking if diminishing returns set in beyond depth=3.

Try WM=2,WN=4 with WTM=2,WTN=4 — asymmetric block tiles favoring the N dimension. For a row-major C output, wider N tiles may enable better vectorized stores. Combined with pipeline depth=2 to isolate the tile shape effect.
Double-buffering with the asymmetric WM=2,WN=4 tile to test N-wide vs M-wide tile preference.
Re-testing the best configuration (WM=4,WN=4,WTM=2,WTN=2 + pipeline=2) for a second measurement to verify the vs_default=0.9487 win is reproducible.
Double-buffering: re-running for second measurement confirmation of the best config.
Extreme M-heavy tile: WM=4,WN=1 with WTM=4,WTN=2. Very tall block tiles favour reuse of A rows. May expose a regime not yet explored.
Using depth=4 with the extreme tile shape to see if deep pipelining can compensate for narrow N tiles by fully overlapping memory and compute.

Start with the largest WMMA warp-tile (WM=4,WN=4 macro tiles with WTM=2,WTN=4 warp sub-tiles) to maximise register reuse and Tensor Core utilisation per SM. For 2048×2048 on 30 SMs, a large tile lets each SM chew through more work per wave, hiding memory latency and filling the 16×16 WMMA fragments efficiently.

Try the transposed-aspect large tile (WTM=4,WTN=2 vs WTM=2,WTN=4) — same total work but different M vs N warp-partition, which can improve coalescing depending on the memory layout of B. Worth comparing both extremes of the WTM/WTN ratio at maximum block size.

Balanced square warp-tile at maximum block size (WM=4,WN=4 with WTM=2,WTN=2). The symmetric partition reduces register pressure compared to asymmetric variants while keeping the largest block tile — a classic sweet-spot for square GEMMs.

Explore medium-M, wide-N macro tile (WM=2,WN=4) with max warp sub-tiles. The smaller M footprint reduces shared memory pressure on the A-tile, potentially allowing higher occupancy on 30 SMs for this square 2048×2048 problem.

Add 3-stage software pipeline to overlap global→shared memory loads with Tensor Core compute. Depth=3 provides two in-flight prefetch stages, which hides the ~100-200 cycle global memory latency typical on Ampere for this tile size.
Re-apply the best-so-far wmma_tile (vs_default=0.9978) and pair it with pipeline_stages=2 to see if double-buffering gives additional latency hiding.

Double-buffering (depth=2) is the standard Ampere pattern for WMMA kernels — it prefetches the next tile while the current tile executes, keeping Tensor Cores fed without the register/shared-mem cost of deeper pipelines.

Explore the tall-thin extreme (WM=4,WN=1) with wide warp N-tiling. This maximises row-reuse of A while keeping B access narrow — may suit the A-row-major layout of a square GEMM where B columns are the bottleneck.

Balanced medium tile (WM=2,WN=2,WTM=2,WTN=2) — 1/4 the block area of the largest tile. This doubles the wave-count on 30 SMs, which can improve occupancy if register pressure was limiting the large tiles.

Try WM=4,WN=4 with minimal M warp-tiling (WTM=1) but maximum N warp-tiling (WTN=4) — this configuration produces the fewest independent M-direction register tiles, reducing register file pressure while maintaining the large N footprint that favours coalesced B reads.

Re-apply the best wmma_tile configuration (vs_default≈0.998) and pair it with pipeline_stages=4 to see if a 4-stage pipeline (3 in-flight prefetch stages) yields meaningful latency hiding beyond depth=2.
Test 4-stage pipeline with the best wmma_tile — deeper pipelining can overcome the higher GMEM latency when the tile is large enough to justify the additional shared memory buffers.
Re-apply best wmma_tile and test pipeline_stages=3 to identify whether there's a sweet spot between depth=2 and depth=4 for this tile.
Test depth=3 pipeline (between the noisy 2 and the promising 4) to find if there is a better pipeline depth for this large tile on 30 SMs.

RMSNorm is a row-wise reduction over N=4096. With 256 threads per block, each row needs 4096/256=16 elements per thread — enough arithmetic intensity. We have M=1024 rows → 1024 blocks across 30 SMs (~34 blocks/SM), giving excellent occupancy. This is a solid starting candidate to establish a measured baseline against the default.

512 threads/block: each thread handles 4096/512=8 elements per row. With M=1024 rows we get 1024 blocks dispatched to 30 SMs (~34 blocks/SM). Half-warp-granularity warp count (16 warps/block) gives good warp-level parallelism for the intra-block reduction step and typically matches the default for row-norm on Ampere.

1024 threads/block: each thread handles 4096/1024=4 elements. Max threads per block on Ampere, giving maximum intra-block parallelism for the two-pass reduction (sum-of-squares then normalize). Fewer blocks (1024 total, ~34/SM) but higher parallelism per block — worth measuring as the reduction tree is shallower with more warps (32 warps vs 16).

Completing the full survey: 128 threads/block means 4096/128=32 elements/thread and 1024 blocks. This likely increases register pressure and serializes the reduction more, but it's worth measuring to close out all 4 candidates before deciding.

Vectorizing the inner reduction loop j by 4 enables 128-bit (float4) memory loads for X[i,:] and W[:], maximizing memory bandwidth utilization. With 1024 threads and N=4096, each thread processes 4 elements, so width=4 means one vectorized load per thread — perfectly aligned.

Width=8 (256-bit vector loads) for loop j. With 1024 threads handling 4096 elements, each thread owns 4 elements so width=8 spans across threads — testing whether wider vectorization of the reduction axis helps the memory subsystem on Ampere's 128B cache lines.

Unrolling the inner reduction loop j by 4 reduces loop-control overhead and helps the compiler pipeline memory loads for the sum-of-squares pass. With 4 elements per thread (1024 threads, N=4096), factor=4 means full unroll — may expose ILP in the reduction accumulation.

RMSNorm is a row-wise reduction over N=4096 elements. With 256 threads per block, each thread handles 4096/256=16 elements per row, providing good arithmetic intensity and sufficient warps (8) to hide memory latency. 256 is a classic sweet-spot for reductions on Ampere — enough parallelism without register pressure or occupancy issues.

Try 512 threads: each thread handles 4096/512=8 elements, giving 16 warps per block. Higher thread count may better saturate Ampere's warp scheduler and reduce per-thread register pressure for this memory-bound reduction. Also reduces reduction tree depth, which can lower synchronization overhead.

Try max threads (1024): each handles 4096/1024=4 elements. With M=32 rows and 30 SMs, only ~1 block per SM. Maximum warps per block (32) maximizes warp-level hiding of memory latency. May be best for this small M=32 problem where we need every bit of parallelism.

Try smallest block (128 threads): each thread handles 4096/128=32 elements. With M=32 rows and 30 SMs, more blocks can be scheduled simultaneously (32 blocks total). Higher work-per-thread improves instruction-level parallelism within each thread and may reduce synchronization overhead for the warp shuffle reduction.

For softmax over 4096 columns, 256 threads per block gives 8 warps. Each warp handles a portion of the row reduction, and 256 is a balanced size that allows good warp-level reduction without over-subscribing registers. Starting here to establish the first measured baseline.

512 threads = 16 warps per block. For N=4096 columns, each thread covers 8 elements, which aligns well with warp shuffles for the reduction pass. More threads improve memory bandwidth utilization for this memory-bound operation while staying within Ampere's 1024 thread/block limit.

1024 threads = 32 warps per block (maximum). For N=4096, each thread handles only 4 elements, giving a very fine-grained parallel reduction. On Ampere with 30 SMs, 1024 rows means ~34 blocks/SM, so 1024-thread blocks would give good SM utilization. Trying the maximum to see if more parallelism in the reduction helps.

128 threads = 4 warps per block. For N=4096, each thread handles 32 elements, maximizing register reuse per thread and potentially improving ILP. Fewer warps per block means more blocks can co-reside on each SM, which can improve latency hiding. This is the last block_threads option to survey before deciding.

Vectorizing the inner reduction loop j by 4 enables float4 loads, improving memory bandwidth utilization. For N=4096 with 32-bit floats, width=4 produces 128-bit load instructions which are optimal for Ampere's memory subsystem.
Using 512 threads (the default) as the L3 anchor to force llvm backend routing, so we can measure the effect of L1 decisions in isolation on the llvm backend.
Vectorize the inner j loop by 4 to use 128-bit loads (float4), maximizing memory bandwidth on Ampere's L2/HBM path. N=4096 is divisible by 4, so no remainder handling needed.

Unrolling the j reduction loop by 8 increases ILP by keeping 8 independent accumulator registers in flight simultaneously. For N=4096 with 512 threads (8 elements/thread), factor=8 fully unrolls the per-thread work, eliminating loop overhead.

Placing X in registers keeps the input data in register file across the two passes (max-find and sum-of-exp), avoiding repeated global memory loads. This is the classic online softmax optimization that fuses passes.
Tiling the outer row loop i by 32 creates a 32-row tile that can be dispatched to warps, improving thread reuse and cache locality for the row-wise softmax pattern.

Applying 512-thread block (which equals the llvm default) to force llvm routing and get a clean final vs_default=1.0 measurement confirming no L1 or L3 decision beats the compiler default on this op/shape.

For softmax over N=4096, each thread block handles one row. With 512 threads, each thread processes 4096/512=8 elements — a reasonable register footprint that keeps occupancy high (512 threads = 16 warps/block) while providing enough parallelism to hide memory latency. On a 30-SM Ampere with only 32 rows, we need high per-block occupancy; 512 is a balanced middle ground.

With N=4096 and 1024 threads per block, each thread handles exactly 4 elements. 1024 threads = 32 warps fills a block completely and maximises warp-level reduction efficiency (warp shuffles cover all 32 warps). Given only 32 rows, having maximum intra-block parallelism is critical to saturate the SM. This is the maximum legal block size on this hardware.

Exploring the lower end: 256 threads per block means 16 elements per thread over N=4096. Higher per-thread work can improve arithmetic intensity and reduce synchronisation overhead, but risks register pressure. Must measure against 1024 to understand the occupancy-vs-work trade-off at this small batch size (M=32).

Completing the sweep at the smallest block size (128 threads = 32 elements/thread over N=4096). Likely to be worst due to inadequate reduction parallelism, but needed to confirm the monotonic trend and ensure we don't miss a regime boundary.
